o: x is expressible if it is the OR of some subsequence. We need the smallest positive integer that is not expressible. In example 1, {2,1} expresses 1, 2, and 3, so the answer is 4. In example 2, 1 is missing outright, so the answer is 1. The crucial structural fact: an OR equal to a power of two 2^i can only be produced by elements that themselves are 0 or exactly 2^i, so powers of two must be present individually to be expressible.
k: OR-ing numbers can only turn bits ON, so the expressible numbers are determined by which bits appear.
2^i is expressible iff 2^i itself appears in the array.
If 2^0..2^(i−1) are all present, every value in [1, 2^i − 1] is expressible via ORs of them.

a.i: Put all values in a hash set. Start with x = 1; while x is in the set, double it. The first power of two not in the set is the answer: it is not expressible (only an exact copy of it could produce it), and all smaller positive integers are expressible as ORs of the smaller powers of two that are present.
s: Insert all nums into a hash set.
Set x = 1 and repeatedly double while x is in the set.
Return the first x not found in the set.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build the set plus at most 30 set lookups.

w: The brainteaser insight is that OR cannot clear bits, so a power of two is reachable only from itself. A common wrong approach is trying to BFS all achievable OR values (exponential). Follow-up: what if the array could contain 0? It changes nothing, since OR-ing 0 is a no-op.
